newsitem.title: MEXICO: Old enemies church and state clash in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Old enemies church and state clash in Mexico.

text.p: Mexico's traditional enemies Church and State clashed again on Wednesday after the government threatened to fine the country's top archbishop and close down his cathedral for "meddling" in politics.

The Interior Ministry issued the warning after Mexico City Archbishop Norberto Rivera broke a taboo by saying in a sermon last Sunday that the Catholic church "can and should involve itself in politics as Jesus did." Citizens had the right to disobey authorities who broke the law or flouted human rights, he told his congregation.
In most of Catholic Latin America, such comments would have been unremarkable. But in Mexico, which has a long history of violent Church-state conflict, they were explosive.

The Interior Ministry warned Rivera in a private note sent on Monday to stick to ecclesiastical matters and quoted a constitutional ban on priests opposing Mexico's laws or institutions or making political statements. The text was made public on Wednesday by some local media.

Armando Lopez, the ministry's Director-General of Religious Affairs, told a radio interviewer Rivera faced a fine of about $58,000 and the temporary or permanent closure of his cathedral if he repeated his remarks.

Church sources said on Wednesday the dispute was the most serious between the Catholic hierarchy and the Mexican state since the government of ex-president Carlos Salinas de Gortari changed the constitution in 1992 to let the church recover its legal status and re-established relations with the Vatican.
But the church refused to back down. "What was said (by Rivera), was well said and is maintained and there is no need to change so much as a comma", the archbishopric said.
Reflecting the intense passions unleashed by the church, newspapers across Mexico carried the story in banner front page headlines on Wednesday.

In a Senate debate on Tuesday on the sermon, politicians from the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) excoriated the archbishop, displaying the Mexican nationalists' fiery old anti-clerical rhetoric.

PRD senator Hector Sanchez Lopez, apparently referring to a controversial 1994 meeting between the Papal Nuncio to Mexico, Geronimo Prigione, and two drug traffickers accused of killing a Catholic cardinal, said:
"Would Jesus have approved of the links of some church dignitaries with drug traffickers or of the hefty bank accounts they possess?"

The argument reopened old wounds from a conflict between Mexicans and the Catholic church going back five centuries to the 16th century, when Hernan Cortes and his fellow Spanish conquistadors hurled Indian idols down Aztec temple steps to set up their own altars to the Virgin Mary. Relations have been shaky ever since.

The Catholic church established itself as a pillar of the Spanish Conquest, imposing its doctrine by force on an Indian population who preferred human sacrifice to deities such as Huitzilopochtli, the idol of war, or Tlaloc, god of rain.
Dominican, Franciscan and Jesuit monasteries, dripping with gold and silver, became symbols of the huge economic and political power wielded by bishops in a deeply religious land.

But in the mid-19th century, having shaken off Spanish imperial power, the newly independent Mexican state turned its guns on the church. It confiscated church land, outlawed monasteries, broke relations with the Vatican and scrapped Catholicism as the official religion.
French invaders came to the Church's defence and a civil war ensued.

In this century, the Church came under fire again during the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution, when Indian rebels turned its glittering temples into temporary cowsheds or grain stores. The revolutionary constitution of 1917 put the Church under state control and removed all political rights from ministers, something not modified until Salinas's 1992 initiative.
